questions.question: According to TR22, what role does the APS play in validating an aseptic process?

options.A: The APS is the primary means of validating an aseptic process, and passing it means the process is validated
options.B: The APS is only the final demonstration of the sum of the overall controls and should not be regarded as the primary means of validation
options.C: The APS can replace equipment qualification and sterilization validation, as long as the media fill shows zero positives
options.D: The APS is a mandatory standard, and regulations in every country use the TR22 design as the sole template

questions.explanation: TR22 states that validation of an aseptic process encompasses process design, equipment qualification, the quality system, process controls, monitoring, and personnel training, and that the APS is only the final demonstration of the "sum of the controls" and should not be taken as the primary means of validation. It also cannot replace equipment qualification or sterilization validation; TR22 itself is a guide that establishes no mandatory standard and provides no universal template.

questions.question: Which of the following is explicitly outside the scope of TR22?

options.A: Aseptic formulation and filling of human drugs and biologics
options.B: Formulation and filling operations for veterinary drugs on aseptic lines
options.C: Aseptic filling operations of drugs and biologics in isolators or RABS
options.D: Aseptic operations for sterile bulk and for biotechnology inoculum and feed materials

questions.explanation: TR22 covers aseptic formulation and filling of human and veterinary drugs and biologics; aseptic operations for sterile bulk materials and for biotechnology inoculum and feed materials are outside the scope of the document (see TR28 for APS of sterile bulk).

questions.question: According to the TR22 glossary, what is the key characteristic of a "Campaign"?

options.A: Multiple consecutive batches of the same product (or product family), with no cleaning, disinfection, or decontamination of Grade A between batches
options.B: Different products produced in rotation, with full isolator decontamination between every batch
options.C: A single batch filled over several days, with all parts re-sterilized at the end of each day
options.D: A special production mode used only in media fills and not applicable to consecutive commercial batches

questions.explanation: A campaign is a series of batches of the same product or product family produced in sequence over a period of time, with strict adherence to validated controls, but without cleaning, disinfection, or decontamination of the Grade A environment between batches. The descriptions of rotating products and daily re-sterilization are contrary to "no intermediate decontamination," and a campaign is a commercial production mode, not one used only for APS.

questions.question: Which of the following is a corrective intervention rather than an inherent intervention?

options.A: Aseptic assembly before filling
options.B: Replenishing containers during filling as required by the batch record
options.C: EM sampling in Grade A performed according to procedure
options.D: Clearing a component misfeed

questions.explanation: A corrective intervention is one made to correct or adjust a process in progress, such as clearing a misfeed, adjusting a sensor, or replacing a part, and its frequency of occurrence is not fixed. Aseptic assembly, container replenishment, and EM sampling are inherent interventions required by the batch record or procedures.

questions.question: In what context is "Grade A Air Supply" in the TR22 glossary normally used?

options.A: The critical zone for open product filling, requiring continuous particle monitoring and Grade A microbial limits
options.B: The interior of an isolator, the operating area after VPHP decontamination
options.C: Protecting fully stoppered vials that have not yet been capped
options.D: The personnel gowning room in a Grade B background area

questions.explanation: Grade A air supply is air supplied through filters that produce air of Grade A particle quality, but it does not require continuous total particle monitoring nor does it need to meet Grade A microbial limits; it is used specifically to protect fully stoppered vials that have not yet been capped. The critical zone for open product must fully meet Grade A, and neither the interior of an isolator nor a gowning room is a use under this definition.
questions.reference: PDA TR22 §2.0 Glossary(Grade A Air Supply)

questions.question: Before the initial APS in a new facility, what does TR22 recommend doing first to understand operational problems and the interventions required?

options.A: Run sterility tests on three commercial batches first and schedule the APS after confirming there are no positives
options.B: Combine dynamic environmental qualification with the APS to save time
options.C: Perform engineering batches and/or water trials first
options.D: Simply complete the medium growth promotion test and then proceed directly to the APS

questions.explanation: The initial APS should be performed after equipment, HVAC, sterilization validation, personnel gowning qualification, the EM program, SOPs, and the intervention risk assessment are complete, and it should be preceded by engineering batches and/or water trials to understand operational problems and the interventions needed. For a new facility, combining dynamic environmental qualification with the APS is not recommended; neither sterility tests nor GPT can replace these prerequisites.

questions.question: Which statement about the number and frequency of APS matches the TR22 description?

options.A: 3 consecutive successful runs for a new line; thereafter twice a year for each process, each line, and each shift; at least once a year for each operator
options.B: At least 1 successful run for a new line; thereafter once a year per line; each operator need participate in a successful APS only every two years
options.C: At least 3 consecutive successful runs for a new line; thereafter once a year per line, not separated by shift, with operators participating each year
options.D: At least 5 consecutive successful runs for a new line; thereafter once a quarter; each operator must participate in a successful APS every quarter

questions.explanation: Regulators expect at least 3 consecutive successful APS for a new facility, line, or process (possibly more if it is complex); periodic requalification is twice a year (about every six months) for each aseptic process, each filling line, and each shift, with each operator participating in at least one successful APS per year. A frequency of "once a year per line" is too low or ignores shifts, and "5 consecutive runs, once a quarter" are not TR22 requirements.

questions.question: What is TR22's position on combining dynamic environmental qualification with an APS?

options.A: Prohibited by regulations; the two must always be done separately
options.B: Permitted by regulations, but not recommended for new facilities or where the reliability of environmental control is not yet known
options.C: TR22 recommends it for all new facilities, to obtain the most realistic data
options.D: Only isolators may combine them; RABS and conventional lines may not

questions.explanation: TR22 states that the regulations permit combining the two, but it is not recommended for new facilities or in general where the reliability of environmental control is not yet known. It is neither prohibited across the board nor a recommended practice, and TR22 does not differentiate this provision by isolator or RABS.

questions.question: Which of the following is a worst-case condition recognized by TR22 for inclusion in an APS?

options.A: Deliberately simulating equipment failure to challenge the worst-case scenario
options.B: Including interventions that the risk assessment has judged to carry unacceptable risk
options.C: Having more personnel enter the aseptic area than the routine production maximum
options.D: The largest container with the slowest filling speed, giving the longest exposure time of the container opening

questions.explanation: Worst case is an extreme condition within the range allowed for the routine process, such as the longest post-sterilization hold time, the maximum number of personnel, or the largest container at the slowest speed. Equipment failure is a deviation, interventions of unacceptable risk should not be included, and the number of personnel should be only what routine processing would use, never more.

questions.question: Under the TR22 risk assessment principles, how should the number of units filled in an APS be adjusted for the process design?

options.A: Labor-intensive lines should use more units, typically approaching the full production batch size
options.B: All technologies always use the same number of units, regardless of process design and contamination risk
options.C: Isolators, being low risk, can be exempted from APS entirely
options.D: Labor-intensive lines have many interventions and should reduce the number of units to lower the incubation and inspection burden

questions.explanation: When the process design makes contamination more likely (for example, a labor-intensive filling line), more units should be used, typically approaching the full batch size; an isolator lacks direct personnel intervention and can use a smaller number of units as a proportion of the overall operation, but an APS is still required. The number of units is adjusted by risk, is not a fixed value, and must not be reduced because of the incubation burden.

questions.question: Some permitted corrective interventions occur in fewer than 50% of batches. How does TR22 recommend challenging them in the APS?

options.A: Perform each at least once in every APS, to ensure every permitted intervention is challenged each time
options.B: Never include them in the APS, as long as a written procedure exists
options.C: Repeat each in every APS up to the maximum number of times it may occur in production
options.D: Rank them by risk and frequency of occurrence, ensuring each is included at least once a year

questions.explanation: If all infrequent interventions were included in every APS, the overall intervention rate would be pushed to an unrepresentative level. TR22 recommends ranking them by risk and frequency, ensuring each permitted intervention is included at least annually, so a low-risk, low-frequency intervention can be challenged once a year rather than every six months. The number of repetitions need only be representative and does not have to equal the maximum in production.

questions.question: In an APS, for integral units removed after an intervention per procedure, if the decision is to incubate them, how does TR22 require them to be handled?

options.A: Incubated together with the normal units and counted toward the APS acceptance criteria and contamination rate
options.B: Incubated separately and not included in the acceptance criteria, but the root cause must still be investigated if contamination is found
options.C: They must never be incubated, so as not to interfere with the evaluation
options.D: More units may be removed than in production, to be safe

questions.explanation: Units rejected in connection with interventions may be incubated for their informational value, but they should be incubated separately and not counted toward the APS acceptance criteria; if contamination is found, the root cause is still to be investigated, the impact assessed, and corrective action taken. TR22 encourages incubating them when there is scientific value, and the number of units removed or the extent of line clearance in an APS must never exceed that in production.

questions.question: When simulating a conventional lyophilization process, how should the chamber pressure be set?

options.A: Exactly the full-cycle production deep vacuum, to represent real conditions
options.B: Freeze the media first and then pull a vacuum, to fully simulate the freezing step of lyophilization
options.C: Not lower than the equilibrium vapor pressure of the media; best practice is about 100-200 mbar
options.D: Pressure is not important, as long as the vacuum hold time equals the production dwell time

questions.explanation: A vacuum that is too deep makes the media boil and overflow, invalidating the simulation; the chamber pressure must not be lower than the equilibrium vapor pressure of the media at the loaded temperature (for example, about 32 mbar for water at 25 °C), and best practice is to maintain about 100-200 mbar during the sublimation and secondary drying simulation. The full process vacuum should not be used, and the media must not be frozen (which would inhibit microbial growth).

questions.question: Nitrogen is used to break the vacuum in lyophilization production. If neither EM nor sterility tests have detected strict anaerobes and the process is not anaerobic throughout, how should the lyophilization APS be designed?

options.A: Use SCDM and break the vacuum with air instead of inert gas
options.B: Switch to fluid thioglycollate medium and continue to use nitrogen
options.C: Use SCDM and nitrogen as in production, with no change
options.D: Use both media, filling half the units with each

questions.explanation: The use of nitrogen does not necessarily constitute the anaerobic conditions that require an anaerobic medium. Inert gas with an anaerobic medium is appropriate only when strict anaerobes are confirmed to be persistently present or the process is anaerobic throughout. Otherwise the lyophilization APS should be run under fully aerobic conditions, that is, with SCDM and air in place of inert gas to break the vacuum.

questions.question: Which statement is correct when empty vials are interspersed in a large-batch isolator APS?

options.A: Interventions performed during the empty vials count toward the number of interventions required during the media fill
options.B: Only units filled with media count toward the APS acceptance requirements
options.C: Empty vials need not be distinguished from media units in the unit reconciliation
options.D: Interventions during the empty vials need not be recorded or evaluated

questions.explanation: Empty vials can bring the mechanical and environmental challenge closer to normal operation without making the APS excessively large, but with limits: interventions during the empty vials do not count toward the intervention requirements during the media fill, and they must still be executed correctly, recorded, and evaluated; reconciliation must clearly distinguish media units from empty vials; and only media units count toward the acceptance requirements.

questions.question: What does TR22 require regarding the APS protocol (or procedure/batch instructions)?

options.A: It must be written, approved by the Quality Unit, and issued before starting
options.B: The APS may be run first, with the protocol written afterward and approved by the Quality Unit
options.C: Only Production management needs to approve it, with the Quality Unit signing only the final report
options.D: A general APS SOP is sufficient, with no need to prepare or approve a document for each APS

questions.explanation: The formal protocol, procedure, or batch instructions describing the APS activities and conditions must be prepared, approved, and issued before the study begins, and approved by a Quality Unit representative before execution; whether other stakeholders review it is up to the company. Writing it after the fact, omitting Quality Unit approval, or preparing no document at all does not meet the requirement.

questions.topic: Recording interventions in the batch record
questions.question: When the APS batch record documents each intervention or stoppage, what information does TR22 require at a minimum?

options.A: Only the total number of interventions
options.B: The type of intervention and the person who performed it, with the time omitted
options.C: The type of intervention, the time of occurrence, the operators involved, the duration, and the box or tray number being filled at the time
options.D: Only corrective interventions, with inherent interventions not needing to be recorded

questions.explanation: All interventions (inherent and corrective) and stoppages must be recorded with the type, time of occurrence, aseptic operators involved, duration, and the box or tray number being filled at the time, so that positive units can later be linked to events. Recording only the total, omitting times, or recording only corrective interventions is insufficient.

questions.question: A contaminated unit is found in an APS, but it is non-integral (incomplete seal). How should this be viewed according to the TR22 final report guidance?

options.A: Non-integral units never count and are simply excluded from the results, with no investigation or documentation
options.B: The APS is always judged a failure, with no need to understand the cause of the integrity failure
options.C: It is enough to note it as non-integral in the final report, with no supporting documentation needed
options.D: The root cause of the integrity failure should be carefully investigated and documented; if it is unrelated to the routine process, it does not necessarily count as a failure

questions.explanation: TR22 notes that contaminated non-integral units require careful investigation and appropriate documentation to support the determination of the root cause of the integrity failure; if the root cause is unrelated to the routine process, it does not necessarily mean failure. Excluding them outright or always judging failure both skip the investigation, and merely noting without supporting evidence is not enough.

questions.question: What is TR22's position on video recording of APS?

options.A: Both FDA and EMA list it as mandatory, and recording can replace direct observation
options.B: It is recommended but not an FDA/EMA requirement; if used, it should accompany real-time observation
options.C: Recording is discouraged, because cameras add contamination risk
options.D: Recording needs to begin only when an APS fails

questions.explanation: TR22 recommends video recording but it is currently not an FDA or EMA regulatory requirement; if used, it should be combined with real-time personnel observation, with a procedure defining its purpose, use, and retention period. Recording cannot replace direct observation; TR22 sees cameras as an advantage (observation is less constrained) and not as a source of contamination; and one value of recording is that techniques can be reviewed afterward regardless of the APS result and that it helps failure investigations, so recording does not begin only after a failure.

questions.question: During an APS, EM exceeded the action limit, but all media units are sterile. How does TR22 view this?

options.A: The APS automatically fails and must be repeated immediately, with all production suspended
options.B: The APS passes, demonstrating that the process can be routinely operated in an environment at that EM level
options.C: The EM investigation must be completed before the APS report is approved, and whether it affects the result is determined by the investigation
options.D: The higher EM result can be set directly as the new alert and action limit for production

questions.explanation: The investigation of an EM excursion should be completed and approved before the APS report is approved; an EM excursion is not automatic grounds for rejecting the APS, and the outcome depends on the investigation. A "pass" of the APS in an environment exceeding the action limit also cannot be used to show that the process can be routinely run in such an environment, and the EM result does not become a new production limit.

questions.question: Routine production uses nitrogen for blanketing and for pressurizing the liquid transfer, and the APS uses SCDM. How should this be handled?

options.A: Continue to use nitrogen, because nitrogen already provides a true anaerobic environment and will not affect the results
options.B: Use sterile-filtered air instead, supplied through the same delivery system
options.C: Eliminate the gassing step entirely, so that the inert gas does not inhibit microbial growth
options.D: Continue to use nitrogen, and confirm the sterility of the inert gas system from the APS results

questions.explanation: Nitrogen does not constitute a true anaerobic environment (anaerobic requires residual oxygen below 0.1%), but used with SCDM it may still inhibit growth, so sterile-filtered air should be used instead, supplied through the same delivery system so that the blanketing and delivery setup is fully simulated. Eliminating the step would miss a process variable; the sterility of the gas system is assured by filter validation, integrity testing, and sterilization of downstream piping, not by the APS.

questions.question: Which statement about the fill volume of an APS is correct?

options.A: It must be exactly the same as the production fill volume, with no partial fill and no overfill
options.B: Any liquid is enough, even filling to the neck of the vial, with no need to consider headspace
options.C: It may be a partial fill, omitting the fill weight adjustment step used in production to save time
options.D: It may be a partial fill, but the media must contact all sealing surfaces when inverted and rotated, and the headspace must be sufficient to support growth

questions.explanation: An APS need not be filled to the normal fill volume, but the media must be sufficient to contact all container sealing surfaces when inverted and rotated, sufficient to detect growth, and even at maximum fill there must be enough air headspace for microorganisms to grow. Whatever the fill volume, fill weight/volume adjustment should be done the same way as in production; a full fill is considered only if it poses no risk of splashing or foaming.

questions.question: What is the general reference value TR22 gives for the number of units filled in an APS?

options.A: Usually at least 5,000-10,000; for batch sizes below 5,000, at least the batch size
options.B: A fixed 3,000 units, regardless of production batch size, technology, or risk
options.C: Always equal to the maximum production batch size
options.D: Usually at least 1,000 units; for batch sizes below 5,000, only half the batch need be filled

questions.explanation: Under EU Annex 1, the number of units must be sufficient to simulate all representative activities, with the rationale written into the CCS. TR22 indicates that typically at least 5,000-10,000 units are filled; where the production batch is smaller (for example, below 5,000), the number of APS containers is at least equal to the production batch size. These are only general reference values and each company still has to justify its own; a fixed value, always a full batch, or half a batch are not TR22 statements.

questions.question: If APS units are incubated at two temperatures, what does TR22 require?

options.A: 7 days in total across both temperatures, higher temperature first and then lower
options.B: 14 days in total, with the days at the two temperatures allocated freely
options.C: At least 7 days at each temperature, lower temperature first, taking into account the time needed for warming up
options.D: 7 days at 30-35 °C first, then 7 days at 20-25 °C

questions.explanation: APS units are incubated for at least 14 days at a temperature within 20-35 °C that is supported by data. If more than one temperature is used, each should be for at least 7 days, starting with the lower temperature (for example, 7 days at 20-25 °C and then 7 days at 30-35 °C), and the warm-up time should be determined to ensure the second temperature gets a full incubation period. The sequences "high then low" and "30-35 °C first, then 20-25 °C" are in the wrong order, and "days allocated freely" lacks the minimum of 7 days at each temperature.

questions.question: During pre-incubation inspection of APS units, some units have cosmetic defects, visible particles, or low fill volume, but the seal is intact. How should they be handled?

options.A: As in production inspection, reject all units with any defect and do not incubate them
options.B: Reject and incubate them separately, without counting them in the APS contamination rate
options.C: Incubate only those with low fill volume and reject the others
options.D: Incubate as usual and count them in the APS evaluation and contamination rate

questions.explanation: Pre-incubation inspection removes only non-integral units (for example, missing caps, cracked glass, poor crimps), because they have no scientific value. Cosmetic, particulate, fill volume, and other defects unrelated to container integrity should be ignored in an APS; these units should be incubated and counted in the evaluation and contamination rate.

questions.question: How should gowning qualification for personnel Qualification Level 1 (L-1) be carried out?

options.A: Only an online course and test need be completed, with no actual gowning or microbiological assessment
options.B: Participating directly in one successful APS completes it
options.C: First visually confirm correct donning of sterile garments, and finally confirm compliance with sterile standards by microbiological assessment
options.D: A supervisor's signature certifying that the person has received gowning training is enough

questions.explanation: L-1 is the foundational stage for entering the cleanroom: classroom or computer-based theory training and competency assessment come first, and the gowning qualification then starts with visual inspection of whether sterile garments can be donned correctly, finally confirming compliance with sterile standards by microbiological assessment. A test alone or a supervisor's signature is insufficient, and participation in an APS is an L-3 requirement.

questions.question: What is the final step to reach Level 3 (L-3), able to perform critical aseptic interventions independently with minimal supervision?

options.A: Successfully participating in an APS, with all personnel performing the same roles as in routine production
options.B: Completing three simulated operations in a Grade D area, signed off by a supervisor
options.C: Passing a written exam, with no actual operation in the cleanroom needed
options.D: Completing one water trial under the direct supervision of a supervisor

questions.explanation: L-3 requires demonstrating consistent aseptic behavior and a good trend in personnel monitoring, and finally successful participation in an APS with all personnel performing the same roles as in routine production. Simulations such as water fills are part of L-3 training and not the final gate; a water trial under direct supervision belongs to L-2; and a written exam or practice in a Grade D area is not sufficient for L-3 qualification.

questions.question: An APS has positive units, and the investigation still cannot find the cause. How should this be handled according to TR22?

options.A: Not finding a cause means there is no problem with the process, and the APS can be accepted directly
options.B: Identify the most probable root cause and address it before the APS is repeated, and assess the impact on previous batches
options.C: As long as the positives are below 0.1% of the units filled, it can be judged a pass
options.D: Immediately repeat the APS three times, without first identifying or addressing any cause

questions.explanation: The APS acceptance criterion is zero positives, regardless of the number of units. Not finding a cause does not mean the process is acceptable; the most probable root cause should be identified and addressed before the APS is repeated, with the impact on batches produced before the APS considered. A percentage-based criterion is not the TR22 approach, and repeating the APS over and over without correcting a cause is not enough.

questions.question: After an APS failure, once the investigation and CAPA are complete, how many APS runs are usually repeated?

options.A: 1 run is enough, because the CAPA is complete and has been approved by QA
options.B: 2 runs, the same as the annual periodic frequency
options.C: No repeat is needed; the effectiveness of the CAPA is shown by subsequent EM trends
options.D: Determined by risk, usually 3, unless it is clearly demonstrated that the failure was not a process failure

questions.explanation: The number of repeat runs after a failure investigation and CAPA should be determined by risk, depending on the impact of the changes and how clear the root cause determination is; usually 3 are performed, unless there is clear evidence that the positive units were not caused by a failure of the aseptic process. Repeating is also to confirm that the CAPA is effective and has no unintended consequences, which cannot rest on EM trends alone.

questions.question: An APS was discontinued because of a power outage, and the units filled before the stop were all sterile after incubation. Can this APS be counted as a pass?

options.A: Not necessarily; it cannot be counted as a pass unless the required number of units has been reached and all other conditions and requirements are met
options.B: Yes, as long as there are no positive units after incubation
options.C: No, and the units filled before the stop need not be incubated
options.D: Yes, but the result must be approved by the Production manager alone

questions.explanation: An APS may be discontinued only in situations that would also stop actual production, with authorization from senior production and quality management. Units filled before the stop must be incubated and evaluated; if there are positives (and they are unrelated to the stopping event), the APS may be judged a failure; if there are none, it can count as a pass only if the required number of units was reached and all other requirements were met. Approval by the Production manager alone does not meet the requirement.

questions.question: An APS failure was attributed to an intermittent equipment fault that neither routine maintenance nor operation could detect. When assessing the impact on batches already produced, how far back should the look-back go?

options.A: Only back to the last successful APS
options.B: Back to the last maintenance record showing the equipment was functioning properly
options.C: Only the batches produced on the day of the failure and the day before
options.D: All batches still within their expiry dating may need to be assessed

questions.explanation: The look-back scope should be determined by the failure scenario and root cause. If the fault would readily have been found in routine maintenance, the look-back can go back to the last maintenance that showed the equipment was functioning properly; but for an intermittent fault that neither maintenance nor operation could detect, going back to the last successful APS is meaningless, and all batches within their expiry dating may need to be assessed.

questions.question: An APS failure was attributed to a problem with the lyophilizer. How should the scope of the impact assessment be defined?

options.A: Only all products on the filling line where the failure occurred
options.B: Only all batches of the same product and the same dosage form
options.C: All products that passed through that lyophilizer, regardless of which line they were filled on
options.D: All products in the entire plant, regardless of whether they used that lyophilizer

questions.explanation: A failure on one line does not mean the assessment is limited to that line. If the problem lies in the lyophilizer, any product that passed through it must be assumed potentially affected, regardless of which line it was filled on; conversely, products on the same line that did not use that lyophilizer can be excluded. The choice of time frame and scope must both be justified.

questions.question: What does TR22 require for microbial identification of APS positive units?

options.A: At least to species, with strain typing recommended; for heavy contamination, statistical sampling may be used
options.B: Only to genus is needed, then compare with the EM database
options.C: Only a Gram stain is needed, to judge whether the flora is of human origin
options.D: Every positive unit must be strain typed, without exception

questions.explanation: All positive units should be identified at least to species, with strain typing or a similar method recommended, and compared with the EM database, sterility and bioburden tests, and isolates from earlier APS. With heavy contamination, identifying every vial is impractical and a statistically representative plan may be used. Genus level or a Gram stain is not enough; strain typing is a recommendation, not mandatory for every vial.

questions.question: An investigation confirms that the APS positive was caused by laboratory error or the use of non-sterile media, and is unrelated to the aseptic process itself. How should this APS be handled?

options.A: Judge it an APS failure, requiring CAPA to be completed and then three consecutive APS repeats
options.B: Treat it as invalidated, and replace it with one APS
options.C: Treat it as a pass, with no replacement APS needed
options.D: Keep the original result and explain it only in the annual product quality review

questions.explanation: If the investigation confirms that the cause of contamination is unrelated to the performance of the aseptic process (for example, laboratory error or non-sterile media), the aseptic process has not been judged unacceptable, but this APS should be considered invalid and replaced with one APS. It is not a failure, so three repeats are not required, and it cannot be counted as a pass or merely mentioned in a report.

questions.question: Which statement about APS within ongoing process evaluation is correct?

options.A: Time alone drives it, once every six months, and no change requires an additional APS
options.B: Each periodic APS must always be three consecutive runs
options.C: Once every six months; a single run suffices when there is no change and no contrary evidence, and significant events call for additional APS
options.D: Dissimilar equipment (for example, a rotary piston pump and a peristaltic pump) can always be bracketed, with no need to rotate

questions.explanation: A periodic APS is about every six months, and when there is no process change and no contrary evidence, a single run is sufficient. An APS should also not be driven by time alone: process or equipment changes, major maintenance, before and after a shutdown, long idle periods, dismantling or relocating a line, and after an APS failure or major deviation may call for an event-driven APS. Bracketing may not be appropriate for dissimilar equipment, in which case it can be rotated, with each type challenged at least once a year.

questions.question: For APS of powder filling, suspensions, or ointments, which set of placebo materials does TR22 mention as having been used successfully?

options.A: Lactose, mannitol, PEG 6000, NaCl
options.B: Dry sterile culture medium powder, because its flow properties are closest to the drug powder
options.C: Talc and silicon dioxide, because they are low cost and can be used without separate sterilization
options.D: The actual drug powder, as long as it has been sterilized by a validated method beforehand

questions.explanation: Dry sterile culture medium has been shown to work less well for these operations because of its poor flowability; lactose, mannitol, PEG 6000, and sodium chloride have been used successfully as long as they do not affect microbial growth. A placebo must be sterile (sterilized by a validated method), dispersible or soluble, and non-inhibitory to growth, so a material that "needs no sterilization" does not meet this, and using the actual drug powder is not how a placebo works.

questions.question: If the media starts at double strength and is only later diluted to the final concentration, how should the growth promotion test be arranged?

options.A: Test only the final diluted concentration
options.B: Test only the initial double-strength concentration
options.C: Concentration does not affect the GPT result, so either can be tested
options.D: Challenge both the initial and the final concentration with GPT

questions.explanation: GPT of the surrogate and media combination should be performed by pharmacopoeial methods, considering inclusion of in-house isolates from EM, personnel monitoring, and sterility test failures. If the initial concentration differs from the final concentration (for example, double strength because of subsequent dilution), the initial concentration must also be challenged in GPT.

questions.question: When SCDM is sterilized by moist heat, what range of F0 does TR22 consider generally sufficient, and what is the risk of over-sterilization?

options.A: F0 of about 5-10 minutes; over-sterilization mainly causes the pH of the medium to rise noticeably
options.B: F0 of about 15-20 minutes; excessive time or heat may cause the Maillard reaction
options.C: F0 of at least 60 minutes; under-sterilization is the only concern
options.D: F0 of about 15-20 minutes; over-sterilization affects only the color and appearance, not growth

questions.explanation: An F0 of 15-20 minutes is generally sufficient; longer or hotter cycles that deliver higher lethality may cause the Maillard reaction (including caramelization), impairing the growth-promoting ability of the media. The values "F0 of about 5-10 minutes" and "F0 of at least 60 minutes" are wrong, and "over-sterilization affects only appearance" is wrong in assuming over-sterilization does not affect growth.

questions.question: If media raw materials are suspected of carrying mycoplasma, what sterilization approach does TR22 recommend?

options.A: Ordinary 0.2 µm sterilizing filtration completely removes mycoplasma
options.B: Simply dissolve the medium in hot water above 60 °C
options.C: Moist heat or radiation sterilization; if filtration is used, consider a 0.1 µm membrane
options.D: Extend the media hold time, letting the mycoplasma inactivate naturally before use

questions.explanation: Mycoplasma may not be removed by ordinary filtration, so moist heat or radiation sterilization can be used; if filtration is chosen, 0.1 µm mycoplasma-retentive filtration may need to be considered. Hot water above 60 °C only reduces the bioburden risk from vegetative bacteria and fungi and aids dissolution, and is not a sterilization method; media that are not fully sterile should have their hold time kept as short as possible, not extended.

questions.question: According to the TR22 Appendix 2 APS performance sequence checklist, what is required of the APS batch record?

options.A: Approved by the QU; if the commercial batch record is electronic, the APS should also be electronic
options.B: Always paper, so that electronic system access settings do not affect the APS execution
options.C: Reviewed only by Production, with the Quality Unit involved only at the final report
options.D: It may be omitted, as long as the protocol is approved by the Quality Unit

questions.explanation: Step 3 of Appendix 2 requires preparing an APS batch record that defines the scope and execution requirements and records the actual execution variables, reviewed and approved by the Quality Unit; if the commercial process batch record is electronic, the APS batch record should also be electronic, for consistency with routine production.

questions.question: In the Example 1 risk scoring table, what APS frequency is suggested when the total score is below 15?

options.A: Reduce the process risk first, and have personnel participate every 6 months
options.B: Per-shift frequency may be reduced (for example, every 12 months)
options.C: Every 3 months, with each shift performed separately
options.D: A low-risk process need no longer perform APS, with only EM

questions.explanation: Example 1 scores process complexity, novelty, degree of automation, critical zone protection, personnel experience, and compliance history. A total above 35: reduce the risk first, and if it cannot be reduced (such as a fully manual ATMP), personnel participate every 6 months; 15-35: each shift every 6 months ±1 month; below 15: a lower frequency per shift (for example, every 12 months), as in a mature gloveless isolator process with no human intervention and no OOS history. Even low risk still requires APS.

questions.question: What is the core idea of Example 2 (IREM)?

options.A: A high-risk intervention can be made less risky in production simply by including it in every APS
options.B: The number of interventions is always set to the theoretical maximum, regardless of the previous year's production trends
options.C: Including an intervention in the APS does not reduce its risk; procedural or engineering improvements should come first
options.D: IREM applies only to isolators and not to RABS or conventional lines

questions.explanation: Example 2 points out that including a high-risk intervention in the APS does not reduce its risk in the aseptic process, so after IREM, procedural or engineering improvements should be evaluated (for example, adding a glove port to an oRABS so that an operation that required opening the door is done with the door closed), followed by a reassessment of the risk; the number of interventions is set from the actual trends of the previous year of commercial production. The example itself is an oRABS line, so the claim that IREM applies only to isolators is wrong.

questions.question: In the recommendation table of Example 3, what are the simulation frequency and number for a "low risk" intervention?

options.A: Every six months, with a number at least equal to routine production
options.B: Every six months, with a number that may be less than routine production
options.C: In every APS, with twice the number of routine production
options.D: Once a year, with a number that may be less than routine production

questions.explanation: According to Table 15.3-2: high-risk interventions are simulated every six months, with a number at least equal to routine production; medium-risk interventions are simulated every six months, with a number that may be less than routine production; low-risk interventions are simulated yearly, with a number that may be less than routine production. "Every six months, at least equal to routine production" is the high-risk recommendation, "every six months, less than routine production" is the medium-risk recommendation, and doubling the number is not the TR22 approach.

questions.question: A line fills 2, 4, 8, and 10 mL vials, and the assessment finds that none is a worst case. How should the number of initial validation APS runs be arranged?

options.A: At least 3 runs each for the smallest and largest vial sizes, and at least 1 run for each of the others
options.B: 3 runs for each vial size, 12 initial APS runs in total
options.C: Only 3 runs of the largest vial size (10 mL)
options.D: 1 run for each vial size, 4 initial APS runs in total

questions.explanation: Example 5 states that when there is no worst-case vial size, the smallest and the largest vial sizes get at least 3 runs each, plus at least 1 run for each of the others. If one vial size is the worst case (for example, 10 mL), that size gets at least 3 runs and the others at least 1 each. A vial size added later that falls between the two ends and is not a worst case (for example, 6 mL) needs at least 1 run.

questions.question: In Example 7, after initial validation of an isolator line running four-batch campaigns, how is periodic revalidation designed?

options.A: Every six months, a full campaign simulation of four consecutive media batches, run entirely as in production
options.B: Only a piggyback APS at the end of the campaign, once a year
options.C: One single-batch APS a year is enough, with no need to simulate the campaign length and end
options.D: A single batch (including setup) plus an end-of-campaign piggyback, each every six months

questions.explanation: Periodic revalidation consists of two kinds of APS: a single-batch APS including the full setup and end, and a piggyback APS in which a media batch follows four batches of product, used to simulate the worst case of duration; both are repeated every six months, so the line has 4 APS in total per year, covering the start and end of the campaign. A piggyback cannot serve alone as APS validation, and four consecutive media batches is the design of the conservative initial validation approach (1A).
